apps.name: Helumi
apps.tagline: More space for your Mac, without buying a new one.
apps.description:
Helumi is a macOS application that adds a cloud drive to Finder with terabytes of space and zero bytes used on your Mac. Files look and open like normal, but they live in the cloud and stream only the parts you need, so large videos start playing instantly. This tool is designed for video editors, photographers, and creators who work with large files and are running out of disk space.

Key Features:

- Adds a Helumi drive in Finder, next to Macintosh HD, with up to 30 TB of space.

- Streams only the part of a file you need, so large videos start in under a second.

- Keeps files off your disk, with an option to keep folders offline.

- Shares files with a link and collects files from anyone.

- Restores deleted files for 30 days and resumes interrupted uploads.

Helumi is a macOS application that gives your Mac terabytes of cloud storage as a normal Finder drive, using zero local disk space. Files stream on demand, so even huge videos open instantly.

apps.name: MacWhisper
apps.tagline: Quickly transcribe audio files into text on your Mac
apps.description:
MacWhisper is a Mac transcription app that uses OpenAI's Whisper and Nvidia Parakeet to turn audio and video into accurate, searchable text in seconds. All transcription runs locally on your device with Metal and GPU acceleration.

Core features:
• Drag-and-drop transcription with up to 300x realtime speeds
• Records meetings, microphone, and system audio with automatic detection
• Speaker recognition, batch transcription, and YouTube video support
• Realtime captions with live translation, plus DeepL subtitle translation
• Integrates with ChatGPT, Claude, Groq, Ollama, and 100+ supported languages

Join thousands of journalists, researchers, students, and creators trusting MacWhisper for fast, private, on-device transcription.

apps.name: Anytype
apps.tagline: Local-first notes as typed objects, with encryption and peer-to-peer sync.
apps.description: Anytype is the notes app in the Logseq guide. It organizes information as typed objects with relations, keeps data local-first, and syncs peer-to-peer. The app has a free plan. Paid memberships add remote storage and sharing limits. Check current prices on anytype.io before you buy.

apps.name: iA Writer
apps.tagline: A focused markdown editor sold as a one-time purchase on the Mac.
apps.description: iA Writer is the writing app in the Ulysses guide. It is a markdown editor built around a calm page and plain-text files. The Mac app is a one-time purchase, sold separately from the iPhone, iPad, and Windows versions. The developer's buy page listed the Mac app at $49.99. Confirm the current price on ia.net before you buy.

apps.name: ClearBar
apps.tagline: Hides third-party menu bar icons and keeps them in one panel.
apps.description: ClearBar hides third-party menu bar icons and keeps those apps in one panel, where you can open a menu or quit the app. The developer says it needs macOS 26 or 27 on Apple silicon. The site listed a launch price of $5, then $12, as a one-time purchase. Check the price on the site before you buy.

apps.name: Lounge
apps.tagline: Hides menu bar icons and opens them from a notch panel.
apps.description: Lounge hides and reveals menu bar icons and opens a panel near the notch, with clipboard history in that panel. The developer says it needs macOS 26 or later. The site did not list a price when this was checked.

apps.name: Alcove
apps.tagline: A notch display for notifications and now playing.
apps.description: Alcove puts notifications, now playing, and status in a notch display styled like the iPhone Dynamic Island. The developer says it needs macOS 15 or later. The site did not list a price when this was checked. It is not a menu bar icon hider.

apps.name: HoldSpeak
apps.tagline: Dictation into any Mac app, on the device, paid once.
apps.description: HoldSpeak types what you say into the Mac app where the cursor is. The developer says transcription stays on the Mac, with no account, and that you pay once after a 7-day trial. It needs Apple silicon and macOS 14.6 or later. The site did not list a dollar price when this was checked.

apps.name: Precis
apps.tagline: On-device dictation that types where the cursor is.
apps.description: Precis types what you say into the app where the cursor is, and the developer says the audio stays on the Mac. The site listed a founding price of $19, then $29, paid once. It says the app needs macOS 26.5 on Apple silicon. Check the price before you buy.

apps.name: Voicera
apps.tagline: Dictation into any app, with a free weekly cap.

apps.name: Shottr

apps.name: Better Shot

apps.name: Clippio

apps.description: Clippio stores clipboard history on the Mac, with search, pins, and text recognition on copied images. The developer says there is no cloud sync. The site listed a one-time price of $6.90 and macOS 13 or later.

apps.tagline: Finds leftover files and large caches you choose to remove.
apps.description: Plumby finds caches, old installers, iPhone backups, and files left behind after an app is dragged to the Trash. The site listed $29 a year or $79 once, and macOS 15 or later. It only removes what you select.

apps.name: Bytesweep
apps.tagline: Shows what is filling the disk, then deletes only what you approve.
apps.description: ByteSweep shows what is using disk space and cleans only what you approve. It is a disk cleaner, not an app uninstaller.

apps.name: ScanMyDisk
apps.tagline: A visual disk space analyzer to see what uses your Mac disk space.
apps.description: ScanMyDisk is a visual disk space analyzer for Mac. It maps storage usage into an interactive visual breakdown, helping you find oversized files, inspect hidden directories, and reclaim free space.

categories.name: Design
paragraphs: Most design happens inside one big app, but the work around it doesn't. Reference piles up, exports scatter across folders, and a surprising share of the day goes to finding a file you already made. The apps in this category cover that surrounding work on macOS.
Each one is here because it does a specific job well, not because it has the longest feature list. Open any app for its pricing, a full description, and a link straight to the developer's own site.
tips: File format support — check it handles what you actually ship, from Figma and Sketch exports to PSD, SVG and RAW, without a conversion step in between.
Offline search — an asset library is only useful if you can find things in it without waiting on a sync to finish.
Annotation speed — screenshot tools vary enormously in how fast you can arrow, blur and label something before sending it.
Licensing — one-time licences are still common in this category, so check before you commit to another subscription.

categories.name: Developer Tools
paragraphs: A Mac development setup is mostly small tools that each remove one daily annoyance: exposing localhost to a webhook, seeing what is really eating the CPU, getting back the snippet you copied an hour ago. This category collects the ones worth the install.
Everything listed runs natively on macOS, Apple Silicon included, and links straight to the developer's own site.
tips: Native or Electron — native apps launch faster and cost far less battery, which matters for anything that sits in the menu bar all day.
Apple Silicon builds — look for a universal or arm64 binary rather than something running under Rosetta.
Data handling — for AI clients and clipboard managers, check whether history stays on device and whether you can bring your own API key.
Pricing model — several tools here are one-time purchases and a few are open source, so a subscription is worth questioning.

categories.name: Productivity
paragraphs: Two apps are listed here, one from each guide. Anytype is for structured, encrypted notes. iA Writer is for focused markdown writing.
Open either app for a short description and a link to the developer's own site. Prices change, so the pricing label is the model, not a receipt.
tips: Where the data lives — notes and transcripts are personal, so check for local storage or your own iCloud rather than someone else's server.
Export — if you cannot get your text out as Markdown or plain files, changing your mind later gets expensive.
Weight — an app you want running all day should be measured in tens of megabytes, not hundreds.
Subscription or one-time — this category has plenty of both, and the one-time options are often the better deal over a few years.

categories.name: Utilities
paragraphs: Utilities are the apps you install once and then forget you installed, right up until you use a Mac without them. Screenshot tools, disk cleaners, recorders, media players and menu bar oddities all live here.
It is the largest category on the site, largely because the versions built into macOS are usually fine but rarely great.
tips: Overlap with macOS — Screenshot, QuickTime and Storage Management already do a version of most of this, so the question is whether the app is meaningfully faster.
Idle cost — a utility that sits in the menu bar should be close to invisible in Activity Monitor.
Permissions — screen recording and full disk access are powerful, so prefer notarized apps that explain each prompt.
Recent updates — check something shipped in the last year, because abandoned utilities tend to break with every macOS release.

posts.title: Best AppCleaner Alternative for Mac (2026)
posts.excerpt: AppCleaner is free and only uninstalls an app. Mole is $19 once and also maps the disk. ByteSweep shows what is using the space and does not uninstall for you.

toc.label: If you still want to uninstall
If the disk is full, not the app
What this page does not claim

posts.html:
An AppCleaner alternative is only worth it if uninstalling one app is not the whole job. Mole uninstalls and maps the disk. ByteSweep does not uninstall for you.

AppCleaner, from FreeMacSoft, is free. You drag in an app, it finds the small files that belong to that app, and you delete the ones you tick. The download page has builds for current macOS and for older versions. If that is all you do, a few times a year, you do not need a paid replacement. The page is freemacsoft.net/appcleaner.

What AppCleaner is actually for

People search for an alternative when the free app feels too small. They want a picture of the whole disk, or they want caches and old backups gone, or they already dragged an app to the Trash and the leftovers are still there. Those are three different jobs. A cleaner that deletes caches will not walk you through uninstalling Slack. An uninstaller will not tell you that an iPhone backup is the thing filling the drive.

If you still want to uninstall

Mole uninstalls an app and reviews the leftover files with it. It also cleans caches, draws a map of what is using the disk, and shows live system stats. The site listed $19 once, updates included, a 14-day refund, and macOS 14 or later. That is the closest paid step up from AppCleaner on this shelf, because uninstalling is still in the product. See mole.fit.

Plumby is aimed at the leftovers and the bulky stuff: caches, macOS installers, old videos, iPhone backups, and files left after you dragged an app to the Trash. It removes only what you select, and personal files start unticked. The site listed $29 a year or $79 once, and macOS 15 or later. It is the wrong buy on an older Mac. Confirm the price on plumby.app.

If the disk is full, not the app

ByteSweep explains what is using the space and waits for you to approve a deletion. The developer says nothing is removed until you say so, and that anything cleaned can be put back for 7 days. The site listed $29.99 once for one computer, a 3-day trial on the Mac, and macOS 14 or later. It does not present itself as the thing you drag an app onto. Use it when the question is "what is this 40 GB," not "how do I remove this app." Read bytesweep.app.

Show what filled the diskYes, a treemapCalls out caches, backups, installersYes, and explains each item

Price we could verify$19 once$29 a year, or $79 once$29.99 once

Which one to install

  • You drag in one app, tick its files, and delete them: stay with free AppCleaner
  • You want that uninstall plus a disk map, in one paid app: Mole
  • The app is already in the Trash and you are hunting leftovers, caches, and old backups, on macOS 15: Plumby

If your goal is seeing what uses space across the entire drive rather than uninstalling an app, read our Mac disk space analyzer guide.

A NotchNook alternative puts something useful in the MacBook notch. NotchDodo and Droppy both list $9.99 once. Alcove is the narrower one already on this shelf.

NotchNook turns the notch into a small desk: music, calendar, notes, to-dos, a timer, and a tray you can drop files on. Its site lists two prices, $15 once or $2 a month, and says one license covers two Macs. It needs macOS 14.6 or later, on Apple silicon or Intel. There is a free trial. Read getnotchnook.com before you pay. The $2 plan only stays useful if you keep paying.

What NotchNook is actually for

This is not a menu-bar hider. Lounge and ClearBar tuck icons away. If your goal is hiding crowded icons, read our Bartender alternative guide. NotchNook and the apps below do the opposite. They give the black cutout a panel. If your Mac has no notch, ask that question first. Droppy says it still draws an island on a notchless display. This page does not claim the others do.

NotchDodo and Droppy

NotchDodo is a hover panel for music, timers, the day's calendar, files, notes, and the clipboard. The site calls the $9.99 purchase a lifetime license and says it needs macOS 14 or later. That is a lower one-time price than NotchNook's $15, for a similar list of tools. Confirm it on notchdodo.com.

Droppy is sold as a Dynamic Island. The developer says that on a Mac without a notch, or on an external display, it uses the island rather than a camera cutout. The site listed $9.99 once, no subscription, and a three-day trial of every feature. It needs macOS 14 or later. See getdroppy.app.

The practical split is the screen. If you only use a notched MacBook, NotchDodo is the one whose site lists the music, calendar, files, and notes in one hover. If you also work on a display with no notch, Droppy is the one that says it still has a place to sit.

Alcove is already on this shelf

Alcove was added with the Bartender guide, and it is a different cut of the same idea. It is a notch display for notifications and now playing, closer to the iPhone island than to a tray of files and notes. The developer says it needs macOS 15 or later. A price was not on the page when that guide was written, so this one does not invent one. Use it if alerts and music are the whole job. Do not expect NotchNook's file tray.

These apps were not lined up on the same Mac. Feature lists are what each developer publishes, and prices move. NotchNook's site is the place to confirm the $15 and $2 figures. If a page disagrees with this guide later, believe the developer.

posts.title: Best Paste Alternative for Mac (2026)
posts.excerpt: Tucket, Clippio, and Maclip keep clipboard history on the Mac and charge once. Paste syncs to iPhone and iPad, and its plans renew.

toc.label: History that stays on the Mac
What this page does not claim

posts.html:
A Paste alternative on this shelf is a clipboard history that stays on the Mac. Tucket, Clippio, and Maclip each charge once. None of them claim to sync an iPhone.

Paste saves what you copy, lets you search it, and pins the bits you reuse. Its pricing page lists $2.49 a month or $29.99 a year, and a 7-day trial. Every plan includes the Mac, iPhone, and iPad apps. A pay-once lifetime plan exists on that page. The dollar amount did not show up in the page text, so this guide does not quote it. Check pasteapp.io/pricing.

What Paste is actually for

If the thing you will miss is copying on the Mac and pasting on the iPhone, stay with Paste. The three apps below do not offer that. They are for the other complaint: a subscription for a history that never leaves the computer.

  • You paste on an iPhone or iPad as well as a Mac: Paste
  • You only need the Mac, and you want one payment: Tucket, Clippio, or Maclip
  • You want the history in the notch: Tucket
  • You want several clips pasted in a row, and password apps ignored: Maclip

History that stays on the Mac

Tucket opens from the MacBook notch and sorts copies by type. The last ten clips can be pasted with a shortcut, without opening the panel. The developer says nothing you copy leaves the Mac. The site listed $10 once, with $15 shown as the regular price, and macOS 14 or later. See trytucket.com.

Clippio is a menu-bar history with search, pins, and text recognition on images you copied. The developer says it stays on the device and does not sync to a cloud. The site listed $6.90 once and macOS 13 or later. That is the lowest price of the three. Confirm it on clippio.siliconapps.dev.

Maclip encrypts the history on the Mac. The developer says clips are not uploaded, that apps such as 1Password and Bitwarden are ignored, and that you can paste several clips in order. The site listed $9.99 once for up to two Macs, a 7-day trial, and macOS 13 or later on Apple silicon or Intel. Read maclip.cc.

Tucket is the notch. Clippio is the smaller bill. Maclip is the one that talks about encryption and about not saving passwords. All three say the history stays on the Mac. Paste's reason to exist, on its own pricing page, is the other devices.

posts.title: Best Screen Studio Alternative for Mac (2026)
posts.excerpt: Screen Charm and ScreenToast zoom after you record. Boom skips the editing timeline. Better Shot is the free recorder already on this shelf.

toc.label: What Screen Studio is actually for
Boom, if you do not want a timeline
Better Shot is already on this shelf
What this page does not claim

posts.html:
A Screen Studio alternative is a recorder that makes a demo look edited. Screen Charm and ScreenToast add the zoom after you stop. Boom never opens a timeline.

Screen Studio records the screen, the camera, and the audio, then animates zooms and smooths the cursor so a product demo does not look like a raw capture. Its site says new licenses are a subscription, and that the old one-time license is no longer sold to new buyers. A current dollar price was not on the homepage. Check screen.studio before you pay.

What Screen Studio is actually for

People looking for a Screen Studio alternative usually want the zoom, not a blank recording. The click should pull the frame in, and the cursor should stop jittering. If you only need a file of the screen with no effects, the built-in macOS recorder is enough, and so is a simpler app. If you need a phone in the shot, that is a different tool and it is not on this list.

Zoom after you record

Screen Charm records the full screen, one window, or an area, plus camera, microphone, and system audio. When the recording ends, it puts a zoom on each click. You can change the zoom or delete it. The site listed $99 once, with $149 shown as the regular price, and said there is no subscription. macOS 14 or later is recommended. Confirm the price on screencharm.com.

ScreenToast is the same kind of recorder, and it goes one step further: it can write a script from what you did on screen and read that script aloud. Zooms land on the clicks. The site listed Pro at $7 a month, or $59 for the year, and said you need Pro to export. It needs macOS 14 or later, on Apple silicon or Intel. See screentoast.com.

Between those two, the split is the voiceover and the bill. Screen Charm is a one-time purchase and leaves the narration to you. ScreenToast will draft the narration and then charge a subscription if you want the file out.

Boom, if you do not want a timeline

Boom records and also presents live, with layout changes and zoom while you are talking. The developer says there is no editing timeline. You trim, then export. It is aimed at calls such as Zoom and Meet as well as a recording. The site offers a free trial and did not list a price. It needs macOS 13 or later. Check boomvideo.app.

Pick Boom if the Screen Studio step you wanted to skip is the edit, not the zoom. Do not pick it if you wanted to adjust every click zoom after the fact. That control is what Screen Charm keeps.

Better Shot is already on this shelf

Better Shot is the free recorder from the CleanShot guide. It records the screen and the camera, and the developer says it can add auto-zoom, with no account and no watermark. It needs macOS 14 or later. It is the one to try before paying $99 or starting a subscription. It is not a dedicated demo studio, and this page is not a timed comparison against Screen Studio.

Side by side

  • You want those zooms and a narration written from the recording: ScreenToast
  • You present live and do not want a timeline afterward: Boom
  • You want to see if a free recorder is enough: Better Shot

posts.title: Best CleanShot X Alternative for Mac (2026)
posts.excerpt: Shottr is the screenshot tool, with scrolling capture and OCR. Better Shot is free and also records. DejaShot only searches shots you already took.

toc.label: What CleanShot X is actually for
Better Shot, if you also record
What this page does not claim

posts.html:
A CleanShot X alternative depends on the shot you need. Shottr is the screenshot tool. Better Shot also records. DejaShot does neither. It searches shots you already have.

CleanShot X is the suite people mean when they say "screenshot app": capture, annotation, scrolling pages, screen recording, and a cloud link. On its pricing page, Basic was $35 once, with a year of updates and 1 GB of cloud, then an optional $19 a year. Pro was $10 per user a month, billed annually, with unlimited cloud. Read cleanshot.com/pricing before you pay. The apps below do not all replace that whole list.

What CleanShot X is actually for

If the missing piece is a still image of a window or a long page, you want a screenshot app. If the missing piece is a video of the screen, you want a recorder, and a still-image tool will feel incomplete. If the shots are already in a folder and you cannot find the one with the error message, you want search, not another capture hotkey.

Shottr, for the screenshot itself

Shottr captures an area, a window, or the full screen, and it can scroll a page or a chat and stitch that into one image. It also reads text and QR codes, measures distances on screen, and picks colors. The site says it runs on macOS 10.15 or later. It does not advertise screen recording.

You can download it free. The purchase page says that copy asks you to upgrade after 30 days. Basic is $12 once, for one person and up to five computers, and a license is required for commercial use. That is a one-time payment, not a subscription. Confirm it on shottr.cc.

Shottr is the closest swap when CleanShot's cloud and video editor are not the reason you opened it. You are paying, if you pay, for the still image and the measuring tools.

Better Shot, if you also record

Better Shot takes the screenshot and the recording. You can mark up a still with arrows and text, and you can record the screen and the camera, then trim the video. The developer says the price is $0, with no account and no watermark, and calls the app open source. It needs macOS 14 or later, on Apple silicon or Intel. See bettershot.site.

This is the one to pick when you wanted CleanShot because it records, not only because it grabs a window. It will not run on a Mac stuck before Sonoma. Shottr will.

DejaShot is a different job

DejaShot does not replace the capture button. It reads the text inside screenshots already in the folders you choose, and it notes which app a new one came from, so you can search by what you remember. The site listed $4.99 and macOS 14 or later. Check dejashot.com.

Install it after you already have a pile of shots and cannot find one. Do not install it expecting a scrolling capture or a recorder.

posts.title: Best Wispr Flow Alternative for Mac (2026)
posts.excerpt: HoldSpeak and Precis dictate on the Mac and say the audio stays there. Voicera streams it, then deletes it. MacWhisper is for recordings, not typing.

toc.label: What Wispr Flow is actually for
On the Mac: HoldSpeak and Precis
Voicera, which sends the audio out
What this page does not claim

posts.html:
A Wispr Flow alternative is a dictation app: you talk, and the text lands where the cursor already is. HoldSpeak and Precis say that happens on the Mac. Voicera sends the audio out.

Wispr Flow does that job across Mac, Windows, and phones. On its pricing page, the free plan included 2,000 words a week on desktop, and Pro was listed at $12 per user a month. Check wisprflow.ai/pricing before you treat that as the bill. This page does not claim to know whether Wispr keeps the audio on your Mac. The apps below are clearer about that.

What Wispr Flow is actually for

People searching for a Wispr Flow alternative usually want to stop typing in email, chat, and notes. They do not want a separate window where they drop an audio file. If the recording already exists, that is a transcription app, and it is the last section of this guide.

  • Text should appear in the app you already have open
  • You care whether the audio leaves the Mac
  • You would rather pay once than subscribe
  • You are transcribing a meeting file you already have: skip to MacWhisper

On the Mac: HoldSpeak and Precis

HoldSpeak uses a key you hold, then types into the Mac app under the cursor. The developer says recording and transcription stay on the device, that your voice is not uploaded, and that there is no account. It needs Apple silicon and macOS 14.6 or later. There is a 7-day trial, then a one-time payment. The site did not show a dollar amount when this was written. Read holdspeak.com before you pay.

Precis is the same kind of tool, with a tighter system requirement. The developer says speech recognition runs on the Mac, that no audio is sent to a server, and that the recording is deleted once the words are typed. The site listed a founding price of $19, then $29, paid once, and said the app needs macOS 26.5 on Apple silicon. Confirm both on myprecis.app.

If both will run on your Mac, the practical difference is the system version and whether you want Precis to reshape the sentence for the app you are in. HoldSpeak is the one that still claims to run on macOS 14.6. Precis, as listed, will not.

Voicera, which sends the audio out

Voicera also types into the app you are using. It does not make the on-device promise. The privacy note says audio streams to speech recognition while you talk and is gone once the text comes back. No recording is kept, according to that page. A free plan was listed at 500 words a week. Pro was listed at $12 a month, or $5 a month on the yearly plan. See voicera.app.

Choose Voicera if a free weekly cap is enough to try dictation, or if you are fine with audio leaving the Mac for the length of the sentence. Do not choose it because you wanted offline dictation. The page we checked does not say it works offline.

MacWhisper is a different job

MacWhisper is already on this shelf, and it is the wrong install if you wanted Wispr Flow. It turns audio and video files, and recordings you make in the app, into text. That is useful for a meeting you already captured. It is not the same as holding a key in Mail and having the sentence appear. People mix the names up because both sit near "Whisper." The jobs are not the same.

posts.title: Best Bartender Alternative for Mac (2026) | PickMacApps
posts.excerpt: Find the best bartender alternative for your workflow. Compare ClearBar and Lounge for hiding menu bar icons, and see when Alcove uses the notch instead.

toc.label: What this page does not claim

posts.html:
Finding the best bartender alternative keeps your macOS menu bar uncluttered when background utilities crowd the screen. ClearBar for Mac and Lounge for Mac hide icons, while Alcove for Mac uses the notch.

Bartender is the app people install when third-party icons crowd the menu bar, and when the MacBook notch covers the ones at the edge. The three apps below are the ones on this shelf that get mentioned for that problem. They are not the same kind of tool.

What you are actually replacing

Bartender's job is small. It tucks menu bar icons away and lets you open them again. If that is the annoyance, you want a hider. If the annoyance is that notifications and music have nowhere to sit, you want something in the notch. Buying a notch toy will not tidy a bar full of icons.

Looking for tools that transform the notch into an interactive application tray? Read our companion NotchNook alternative guide.

  • Too many icons, and you still want each menu one click away: a hider
  • Icons disappearing under the notch: a hider that knows the notch is there
  • Notifications, music, and battery as a small island: a notch display, not a hider

Hiding icons: ClearBar and Lounge

ClearBar for Mac hides third-party menu bar icons and leaves Apple's own items in place. Hidden apps sit in one panel. From that panel you can open an app's menu, see its memory use, or quit it. The developer says it runs on macOS 26 or 27, and only on Apple silicon. The site listed a launch price of $5, then $12, paid once. Read clearbarmac.app before you pay.

Lounge for Mac also hides and shows menu bar icons. Hover near the notch and a panel opens with the hidden icons and the ones still on the bar. Clipboard history is in that panel. The developer says it needs macOS 26 or later. Check bartendermacoslounge.com for the current price.

Between those two, the split is the panel. ClearBar is a list of hidden apps with memory and quit. Lounge is a notch-side panel that also keeps clipboard history.

The notch: Alcove

Alcove for Mac is not a Bartender stand-in. It turns the notch into a small display for notifications, now playing, and status, closer to the iPhone Dynamic Island than to a menu bar manager. The developer says it needs macOS 15 or later. See tryalcove.com.

posts.title: Best Logseq Alternative for Networked Notes (2026)
posts.excerpt: Anytype is the Logseq alternative for private, structured notes. Compare objects, encryption, and sync with Logseq's markdown outliner before you switch.

toc.label: When a Logseq alternative makes sense
Logseq and Anytype, side by side

posts.html:
Anytype is the Logseq alternative for people who want notes stored as objects, not only as an outline, and who want encryption without setting it up themselves.

Logseq is the better fit when the work is a daily outline in plain files. Anytype is the better fit when those notes need fields, links between types of things, and sync that is encrypted by default. This page is a comparison, not a ranking of every notes app.

When a Logseq alternative makes sense

Logseq is already a strong outliner. People usually look past it for a specific gap, not because the outliner is broken. A switch is worth it if you need:

  • A note that has fields, such as author or status, instead of only bullets
  • Encryption that is on without a separate setup step
  • Sync between your own devices that does not depend on a folder you manage
  • Relations between notes, such as a book linked to a person
  • A layout that is closer to a database than to a journal

If none of those are the problem, Logseq does not need replacing.

What Logseq is for

Logseq is a free, open-source outliner. Notes live as Markdown or Org files on your Mac. Pages link to each other, and a graph is built from those links, often starting from a daily note. That file-based setup is the point: you can open the same text in another editor, and you can sync the folder with git or iCloud yourself. Official sync, if you want it, is a separate paid service.

It is a poor match if you wanted each note to be a record with typed fields. You can fake that with properties, but the app is still an outliner.

What Anytype changes

Anytype keeps notes on the device first, then syncs them peer-to-peer. A note can be an object with a type. A book can have an author field and a status, and that author can be its own object. The app is free to start. Paid plans add remote storage and sharing limits, so check current prices on anytype.io before you pay.

The desktop code is published under the Any Source Available License. That is not the same as Logseq's open-source license, so do not treat Anytype as a drop-in open-source project.

Logseq and Anytype, side by side

AnytypeLogseq
Shape of a noteObject with fields and relationsOutline of bullets
EncryptionOn by defaultNot on unless you add it
SyncPeer-to-peer, includedYour own files, or paid Logseq Sync
Files you can open elsewhereExport, not the live formatMarkdown or Org on disk
LicenseSource-availableOpen source
PriceFree to start; storage plans are paidApp is free; official sync is paid
Best fitPrivate notes with structureDaily outline and a graph

Stay with Logseq if

  • You write in bullets and a daily journal
  • You want the notes as plain files in a folder
  • You already sync that folder with git or iCloud
  • You use the graph as the way you find old notes
  • You want an open-source app specifically

Switch to Anytype if

  • You want a book, a person, and a project to be different kinds of notes
  • You want those notes linked by a relation, not only by a wiki-style link
  • You want encryption without a setup step
  • You want sync between devices without running your own folder sync
  • You are fine exporting if you later want plain Markdown

The difference that matters

The useful difference is the shape of a note. In Logseq, a reading log is a page of bullets: title, then author, then a quote. In Anytype, the same log can be a Book object with those as fields, and the author can be a Person object you reuse on the next book. If you will not use fields and relations, you are paying complexity for a feature you will not open.

Which note fits which app

JobUse
Daily journal and a graph of pagesLogseq
Reading list with author and status fieldsAnytype
Notes you must open as .md in another appLogseq
Notes you want encrypted on every device you addAnytype

posts.title: Best Ulysses Alternative for Writing (2026)
posts.excerpt: iA Writer is the Ulysses alternative for focused Markdown and a one-time Mac purchase. Compare the library and the subscription before you switch.

toc.label: When a Ulysses alternative makes sense
Ulysses and iA Writer, side by side

posts.html:
iA Writer is the Ulysses alternative for people who want a Markdown file and a quiet page, bought once on the Mac, instead of a writing library on a subscription.

Ulysses is the better fit when one library has to hold many projects, with goals and publishing built in. iA Writer is the better fit when the draft itself is the whole job. This page compares those two jobs. It does not claim one app is better at everything.

When a Ulysses alternative makes sense

Ulysses is a full writing app for Apple devices. People look for something else when the library, or the subscription, is the part they do not want. A switch is worth it if you need:

  • A page that gets out of the way of the sentence you are writing
  • A Markdown file in a folder, not only inside an app library
  • A Mac purchase you pay once, rather than a subscription
  • The same kind of editor on Windows, not only on Apple devices
  • Less organization around the draft

If you live in the library, sheets, and publishing tools, Ulysses is doing the job you bought it for.

What Ulysses is for

Ulysses is a Markdown writing suite for Mac, iPhone, and iPad. Projects sit in one library. You can set a writing goal, keep notes beside a draft, and publish from the app. Sync stays inside Apple's ecosystem. The app is sold as a subscription, so the cost continues after the first year. Check the developer's current price before you subscribe. This page does not quote it, because that number changes.

What iA Writer changes

iA Writer is a Markdown editor. Focus mode dims every sentence except the one you are in. The file is plain text you can keep in any folder. The Mac version is a separate purchase from the iPhone and iPad version, and from Windows. On the developer's buy page, the Mac app was listed at $49.99. Confirm that before you pay. A purchase covers the current version; major upgrades can cost extra later.

Ulysses and iA Writer, side by side

iA WriterUlysses
Main jobThe sentence in front of youA library of projects
FilesMarkdown in a folder you chooseA library the app manages
DevicesMac, Windows, iPhone, and iPad, sold separatelyApple devices

Stay with Ulysses if

  • You keep many articles or chapters in one library
  • You use writing goals and publishing from the same app
  • You work only on a Mac, iPhone, and iPad
  • You want sheets, keywords, and filters around the draft
  • A subscription is an acceptable way to pay for that library

Switch to iA Writer if

  • You want the current sentence highlighted and the rest dimmed
  • You want the draft as a Markdown file you can move
  • You also write on Windows
  • You would rather pay once per platform than subscribe
  • You do not need a built-in publishing pipeline

The difference that matters

The useful difference is where the draft lives. In Ulysses, a chapter is an item in the library, with a goal count beside it. In iA Writer, the same chapter is a Markdown file in a folder, and focus mode fades the sentences you are not writing. If you will miss the library, iA Writer will feel empty. If the library was the part you were avoiding, that emptiness is the feature.
